paragraphs.text: Elephant Village is a cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, made in 2010. It began as [maocha](sheng:making): large-leaf tea fried in a wok, rolled, then dried in the sun rather than by hot air, which leaves enough of the leaf’s own activity alive for the tea to keep changing for years. That leaf was then [pressed into a cake](sheng:pressing), the compact shape that first let pu’er travel the old trade routes on pack animals.

At sixteen years it is past the ten that some in the trade count as [aged](sheng:ageing), and short of the twenty or more that many others wait for. How far a cake has come depends on how it was pressed and where it was kept, since [heat and humidity](sheng:storage) set the pace of that slow change.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
